item.title: A Provocative Streamer Creates Headaches for El-Sayed in Key Senate Race
item.description:
Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee in Michigan’s pivotal Senate race, has labored for weeks to push past criticism of his relationship with Hasan Piker, a provocative streamer who campaigned with him during the primary.

Dr. El-Sayed has said that he disagrees with Mr. Piker on “many, many things,” and that he doesn’t plan to campaign with him this fall. But he has resisted calls to disavow Mr. Piker more fully.

This week, some of those calls grew, after Mr. Piker said the United States had caused more terror than the group that orchestrated the Sept. 11 attacks. Dr. El-Sayed swiftly rejected the assertion. And Mike Rogers, the Republican Senate nominee in Michigan, issued a statement saying that “enough is enough” and called on Dr. El-Sayed to “condemn Piker once and for all.”

It was the latest episode to underscore the challenge Mr. Piker poses for Dr. El-Sayed, whose race could decide control of the Senate. Mr. Piker, who has a huge, young audience, has sway with the sorts of progressives who powered Dr. El-Sayed’s populist primary campaign. But other Democrats, who say they are appalled by some of Mr. Piker’s criticism of the United States and Israel, have pressured Dr. El-Sayed to go further and fully disavow Mr. Piker. And Mr. Rogers has used Mr. Piker’s incendiary commentary to cast Dr. El-Sayed as outside the mainstream and even un-American.

Dr. El-Sayed has said he campaigned with Mr. Piker during the primary because he wanted to reach Mr. Piker’s audience, which Dr. El-Sayed says is alienated from the political process. He has been repeatedly called to answer for Mr. Piker’s most provocative statements.

The latest came in an interview with Axios on Wednesday. Mr. Piker was asked if he continued to believe the United States was the “top dog” in terrorism, a view he has expressed over the years. The interviewer also asked if Mr. Piker believed the country was responsible for more terror than Al Qaeda, which planned the attacks that killed 2,977 people on Sept. 11, 2001.

“Pound for pound, as far as the number of deaths, yes,” Mr. Piker told Axios. “We have caused tremendous terror all around the world.”

Dr. El-Sayed disagreed.

“I do not agree with this statement, nor do I give much weight to the statements made by a social media streamer,” Dr. El-Sayed said in a statement, adding that he was more focused on the price of gas, groceries and health care. “As I have said, this campaign speaks for itself.”

In a text message, Mr. Piker wrote that “mainstream outlets focus far too much on me as a way to attack” Dr. El-Sayed. He said he was “totally independent” from Dr. El-Sayed and his campaign. On social media, Mr. Piker also defended his comments to Axios, saying that he had given a “nuanced answer.”

In the Axios interview, Mr. Piker pointed to a U.S. strike that hit an elementary school in Iran in February. Iranian officials have said the death toll was at least 175 people, most of them children. A preliminary U.S. investigation determined that the strike on the school was the result of a targeting mistake.

“If you’re killing 140 schoolgirls, that is an act of terror,” Mr. Piker said. “This doesn’t mean that all Americans are terrorists. But the reality of the matter is we have to create an environment of accountability to ensure things like that never happen again.”

Mr. Piker has long criticized America’s engagement in wars in Afghanistan and Iraq, in which hundreds of thousands of civilians died, calling the conflicts “devastating.”

The race between Dr. El-Sayed and Mr. Rogers, a former congressman and an ally of President Trump, is seen as one of a handful competitive races that could determine Senate control.

For weeks, Mr. Rogers has attacked Dr. El-Sayed over his ties to Mr. Piker.

Dr. El-Sayed campaigned with Mr. Piker in April at rallies on two college campuses. The two also appeared together in the final days of the primary race in August, with Mr. Piker joining Dr. El-Sayed’s primary night party in Detroit. Dr. El-Sayed has repeatedly said he has no plans to campaign with Mr. Piker in the general election.

Jewish Democrats, in particular, have been pushing Dr. El-Sayed to disavow Mr. Piker more forcefully. Mr. Piker is a fierce critic of Israel and has called the Hamas-led attack on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, the “direct consequence” of actions by the Israeli and U.S. governments.

A group of Jewish voters in Michigan issued a letter on Wednesday urging support for Dr. El-Sayed. But some Jewish voters have said they are uneasy about his ties to Mr. Piker, and the Michigan Democratic Jewish Caucus has not endorsed him.

At a debate on Tuesday that Mr. Rogers did not attend, Dr. El-Sayed said he disagreed with many of Mr. Piker’s positions, citing, among other things, “his ridiculous comments about 9/11.” But, he said, “I resist the idea that we should play this cancel culture gotcha game that tells us who we can’t talk to.”

In the past, Mr. Piker said the United States “deserved” the Sept. 11 attacks. He later apologized.

item.title: Yosemite Wildfire Grows to Nearly 1,200 Acres
item.description:
A wildfire burning in the backcountry of Yosemite National Park had ballooned to nearly 1,200 acres by Thursday, forcing the closure of several trails and diminishing air quality within the iconic destination.

The fire started on Tuesday about an hour’s drive south from Yosemite Valley, the most-visited section of the park. Firefighters had no containment as of Thursday afternoon, and the cause of the fire was under investigation.

The flames were burning through brush and timber on rugged backcountry slopes, about a quarter-mile from Chilnualna Falls, a series of waterfalls popular with horseback riders in the Wawona area of the park. The park’s largest grove of giant sequoias, including the well-known Grizzly Giant, the oldest tree in the grove, is about five miles south of the nearest edge of the fire, but officials say they aren’t threatened.

Data as of Sept. 17 at 8:03 p.m.. Source: Cal Fire William B. Davis, Madison Dong, Joel Eastwood and Joey K. Lee/The New York Times

The blaze, called the Dome fire, is most likely to spread north, officials said, driven by gusty winds launching embers beyond the fire perimeter. More crews were being flown in Thursday to assist while helicopters continued to drop water on the flames, officials said.

There were no immediate threats to infrastructures or developed areas, officials said.

The Dome fire broke out during dry weather that is typical in the Sierra Nevada in the late summer. With little rain having fallen in recent months, the grass, brush and trees were parched and highly flammable.

Though winds have helped to spread the flames, they have not been extreme enough for the fire to explode. Isolated wind gusts of about 15 to 25 miles per hour were expected in the fire area on Thursday, followed by something of a reprieve on Friday.

“The winds are looking even lower tomorrow compared to what we’re seeing today,” said Matthew Carter, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service office in Hanford, Calif.

On Thursday afternoon, air quality was lower than normal in Yosemite Village, north of the fire, and officials warned people who were particularly sensitive to poor air to reduce outside activity. In many other parts of the park, however, air quality remained high.

The fire came as another burned this week north of Lake Tahoe. That blaze, the Floriston fire, has reached 640 acres and has shut down a westbound section of Interstate 80 near the California-Nevada border.

item.title: Man Who Attacked Ilhan Omar Sentenced to 14 Months After Plea Deal
item.description:
The man charged with squirting vinegar onto Representative Ilhan Omar at an event in Minneapolis this year was sentenced on Thursday to 14 months in prison following a plea deal with federal prosecutors, court records show.

The attack happened in January at a town-hall meeting where Ms. Omar had been calling for the resignation of Kristi Noem, then the homeland security secretary, at the height of the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown in the state.

Prosecutors say the man, Anthony J. Kazmierczak, 56, approached Ms. Omar while she was speaking and sprayed her with apple cider vinegar and water through a syringe. Ms. Omar’s security guards promptly tackled him. Ms. Omar was not hurt.

Mr. Kazmierczak, a Minneapolis resident, pleaded guilty in May to a federal charge of assault. His defense lawyers had asked for him to be sentenced to eight months. He was sentenced on Thursday to 14 months in prison and two years of supervised release, according to court records.

Federal prosecutors, in their sentencing memorandum, called the attack a “serious” offense in an era of growing political violence.

“It was not what we asked for, but it was not out of line either,” Mr. Kazmierczak’s lawyer, John Fossum, said of the sentence.

Mr. Kazmierczak had posted for years about his anger toward Democrats and had shown his support on social media for President Trump and other conservative figures. Before the town hall in January, Mr. Kazmierczak told a neighbor that he might be arrested at an event featuring Ms. Omar.

Ms. Omar, a progressive Democrat, was first elected to represent Minneapolis in 2018. She has been targeted by Mr. Trump for years. He has said that she should “go back” to her native country, Somalia, and has referred to her as “garbage.”

Shortly before Mr. Kazmierczak lunged at Ms. Omar with a syringe, Mr. Trump singled her out at a rally in Iowa, saying that foreigners coming into the United States “have to show they can love our country; they have to be proud — not like Ilhan Omar.”

In a statement on Thursday, Ms. Omar said that she was “grateful to the prosecutors and judge for holding the perpetrator accountable for his actions in January, adding that “political violence or threats are never acceptable.”

Mr. Kazmierczak still faces separate charges in state court. Hennepin County prosecutors charged him with one felony count of making violent threats and a misdemeanor assault charge.

Daniel Borgertpoepping, a spokesman for the office, said prosecutors were weighing whether to proceed with the state case.

“Our office will review Mr. Kazmierczak’s federal case and plea, communicate with the victims and decide on an appropriate path forward,” he said.

Ernesto Londoño contributed reporting.

item.title: Montana Ban Would Strike at Political Spending, and the Supreme Court
item.description:
Voter disgust over an avalanche of political spending by corporations, labor unions and other special-interest groups is driving support for a possible ban on “dark money” in Montana, which could test a landmark Supreme Court decision.

The ballot measure has strong backers from across the political spectrum, including a well-known former Republican governor and Democratic senator who have campaigned for it together.

The main challenge: Threading the needle of Citizens United, the 2010 Supreme Court decision in which a 5-4 majority ruled that independent political spending by corporations and labor unions was a protected form of free speech.

The decision opened a flood of “dark money” that critics blame for coarsening politics and empowering special interests.

“I haven’t talked to a person yet that doesn’t think that there’s too much money in politics,” said Jeff Mangan, a lifelong Montana resident who is the founder and president of the Transparent Election Initiative, the organization behind the proposal.

Montana business groups, the Republican governor and his party are already calling the proposed ballot measure unconstitutional under Citizens United. But supporters believe they have a potentially winning legal argument: Corporate regulations.

Corporations, unions and nonprofits are registered to do business within individual states, which can also impose regulations and restrictions on those entities for the privilege of operating there.

The penalty for violating Montana’s ban on corporate political spending would be to revoke an entity’s corporate registration, making it an issue of state sovereignty, the measure’s supporters argue. They say the state has the right to define corporations as “artificial persons” that lack free speech rights.

“I think it’s creative lawyering, and I don’t mean that in a negative way,” said Justin Levitt, a law professor at Loyola Marymount University in Los Angeles who served in the Biden administration. If the ban passed, it would almost certainly be challenged, with the Supreme Court likely having the final say.

Montana isn’t a place necessarily associated with anti-corporate sentiment or watchdog activism. President Trump won the state by nearly 20 percentage points in 2024, and Republicans are easily the largest bloc of registered voters. But it also has a populist streak and a historical distrust of big institutions.

The ballot question, which goes before voters in November, will ask whether the state should bar businesses, unions and nonprofit groups from making donations to candidates and political parties, or from taking sides in public referendums. It requires support from a simple majority of voters.

If passed, it would take effect on Jan. 1, 2027, making Montana the first state with such a law on the books. Hawaii lawmakers approved a similar prohibition in May, but it does not take effect until July, and is already being challenged in court.

During the 2024 federal election cycle, nearly $2 billion in dark money was spent across the country, according to the Brennan Center for Justice, a voting rights and democracy group. Those donations are largely exempt from individual spending limits and disclosure requirements under Citizens United.

Mr. Mangan, a former Montana commissioner of political practices, a watchdog position in state government overseeing ethics and transparency, said he senses widespread frustration over the political spending and influence of special interests.

“Folks are kind of throwing up their hands,” he said.

The spending ban is opposed by the state’s Republican Party and the Montana Chamber of Commerce, which has about 2,000 members. Todd O’Hair, the group’s president and chief executive, said the restrictions would concentrate more political power in the hands of wealthy individuals.

“We think it’s a clear violation of free speech,” he said.

Gov. Greg Gianforte, a Republican in his second term, has also urged voters to reject the measure. In a statement on Wednesday, Sean Southard, his spokesman, described it as “a likely unconstitutional gag order on Montana small businesses, ranches and family farms.”

But at least one of the state’s former top Republicans is supporting the ban. Marc Racicot was governor from 1993 to 2001, and served as the Republican National Committee chairman in the early 2000s. He appeared at a town hall event on Wednesday in Billings to help promote the initiative alongside Jon Tester, the state’s former Democratic senator.

Mr. Racicot said in an interview that the political system had become “rancid” since Citizens United, with billions of dollars paying for an onslaught of attack ads without identifying the source.

“The money moves around through these serpentine collections of entities and groups, then it becomes unidentifiable,” said Mr. Racicot, who considers himself an independent.

Restrictions on political spending have broad public support, said Tom Moore, a senior fellow for democracy and government at the Center for American Progress, a liberal think tank in Washington that has championed legal arguments for the measure.

“Everybody hates dark money,” he said.

Professor Levitt at Loyola Marymount suggested that even with a ban, though, special interests would still wield outsize influence, as long as wealthy individuals could still give vast sums.

“This wouldn’t change a thing about Elon Musk’s political spending,” he said.

item.title: Trump Wants Putin to End the War. He May Offer Russia Business Deals First.
item.description:
When President Trump’s envoys sat down with Vladimir V. Putin at the Kremlin this month, the Russian leader exuded confidence.

Within months, he said, Russian troops would finally capture Ukraine’s entire Donbas region. And Russia was poised to pummel Ukraine’s electricity grid, setting the stage for a miserable winter.

Then one of the envoys, Jared Kushner, tried to push back. With all due respect, you told us exactly that a year ago, Mr. Kushner said to the Russian president. What are the chances we come back here in another year and you are again saying the same thing? Maybe we don’t lose a year?

The exchange, described by a person familiar with the talks and by a U.S. official, captured the quandary of Mr. Trump’s more than 18 months of efforts to end the war in Ukraine.

Congress this week passed a landmark sanctions bill taking aim at Russia’s energy sector, a new attempt to make Russia “suffer” for its invasion and to pressure Mr. Putin to make compromises.

But even as that bill makes its way to Mr. Trump’s desk, the Trump administration is doubling down on a different approach: offering benefits for Russia that officials hope will get Mr. Putin to consider ending his war.

Among the new inducements: the White House is now considering signing business deals with Russia before it stops fighting in Ukraine, according to two people close to the talks. The U.S. official, speaking on condition of anonymity to be candid about the negotiations, said that deals with Russia before the end of the war were possible because they would show that the United States is serious about a reset relationship with Russia.

The approach represents a shift from Mr. Trump’s pledge last year that business deals with Russia would not come “until we get the war settled.” It indicates that Mr. Trump’s envoys for ending the war, Steve Witkoff and Mr. Kushner, are groping for new ways to entice Russia to stop fighting, now that it has become clear that Ukraine will not withdraw from the swath of its own territory that Mr. Putin insists he must control before the war ends.

And it contrasts with the approach advocated by both Republicans and Democrats in Congress — not to mention Kyiv’s European allies and Ukraine itself — that only heightened economic and military pressure on Mr. Putin can compel him to compromise.

“This bill will cripple Russia’s war machine and finally bring Putin to the negotiating table,” Representative Michael McCaul, Republican of Texas and one of the sanctions bill’s leading proponents, said on Wednesday after a bipartisan majority passed the legislation, 262 to 159.

Mr. Trump has indicated he will sign the bill, which was championed by Senator Lindsey Graham, Republican of South Carolina, until his death in July. It would allow the president to levy tariffs of as much as 100 percent on countries buying the most Russian oil or gas and would impose sanctions on Russian officials, businesspeople and financial institutions. Senator Darline Graham, Mr. Graham’s sister who replaced him in his seat, said it would “increase the president’s negotiating leverage.”

But insofar as the Trump administration is pursuing a carrot-and-stick approach with Mr. Putin, carrots seem the focus. The U.S. official said that the administration wanted to create more incentives for members of the Russian elite to push for peace. Executing some business deals before the end of the war could help convince anti-American hawks around Mr. Putin that Mr. Trump really does want to create a new relationship with Russia, the official added.

Balazs Jarabik, a former European Union diplomat in Kyiv who now works at R. Politik, a political analysis firm, said signs pointed to the United States “considering bigger concessions toward Russia.”

Washington “is now signaling that some deals could move forward if Moscow first demonstrates concrete restraint,” said Mr. Jarabik, who has been tracking the talks closely. “Washington had previously resisted signing such agreements before a cease-fire.”

It was not clear what deals in particular are on the table. The Kremlin’s foreign policy adviser, Yuri Ushakov, said after Mr. Putin’s meeting with Mr. Witkoff and Mr. Kushner on Sept. 5 that “economic issues and potential major mutually beneficial Russian-American projects were discussed in some detail.”

The Kremlin has been promoting business opportunities to the White House ever since Mr. Trump returned to office last year. Russian officials have floated deals for rare earths and aluminum, joint ventures in the Arctic and even getting U.S. companies involved in selling Russian natural gas to Europe.

Mr. Trump has hailed Russia’s economic potential as “tremendous,” but he has previously held out business deals as a reward for a Russia that makes peace.

“They want to do business,” Mr. Trump said ahead of his Alaska summit with Mr. Putin last year. “But they’re not doing business until we get the war settled.”

The quiet shift appears to reflect the administration’s pursuit of new ideas to end the war after talks surrounding a possible Ukrainian withdrawal from the rest of the Donbas region ran aground. Earlier this year, Ukrainian officials proposed calling that area “Donnyland” in an effort to appeal to Mr. Trump to push back harder against Russia’s territorial demands.

Mr. Kushner referred to the impasse in an appearance by video link at a gathering of international supporters of Ukraine in Kyiv last weekend, the YES Annual Meeting.

“President Putin’s laid out his line of what he wants to achieve,” Mr. Kushner said. “If Ukraine, you know, wanted to withdraw to that line, then obviously, we have the rest of the deal set up and put together. Ukraine right now does not want to do that.”

Mr. Kushner went on that the Trump administration’s job “as the mediators” was to “come up with a creative solution” that “allows both parties to move forward.” He said Mr. Trump and President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine were very committed to the talks, and “what we heard is President Putin’s very committed to this as well.”

At that point, part of the audience in Kyiv burst out in laughter, a sign of the deep skepticism among Ukraine’s allies of the administration’s evenhanded portrayal of the talks. Two days later, a jet-powered Russian drone struck a train at a border crossing through which dignitaries, including David Petraeus, the former C.I.A. director, were traveling.

The negotiations to end Russia’s war, which has now lasted more than four and a half years and claimed hundreds of thousands of lives, largely ground to a halt earlier this year as Mr. Witkoff and Mr. Kushner focused on the war with Iran.

This month’s trip to Moscow and then to Kyiv by Mr. Witkoff and Mr. Kushner appeared to be an effort to restart the negotiations. Ukrainian officials said that trilateral peace talks between the United States, Ukraine and Russia could resume in October. The possibility of a limited cease-fire — ending strikes on shipping in the Black Sea or on energy infrastructure — is expected to be discussed in those talks.

Robert Jimison contributed reporting from Washington.

item.title: Blanche’s Political Activity Breaks an Ethical Norm Going Back to Watergate
item.description:
Attorney General Todd Blanche has repeatedly participated in campaign events and spoken in partisan terms about the coming midterm elections since his confirmation last month, despite criticism that he violated a longstanding Justice Department principle of steering clear of electoral politics.

This week he waded again into those waters — twice.

Since August, Mr. Blanche has come under fire for making campaign-tinged public appearances and comments. Last month, at a rally-style event on Long Island, he praised Bruce Blakeman, the Republican candidate for governor of New York. Last week, Mr. Blanche delivered remarks at the Republican Party’s midterm convention.

On Tuesday, he stood at the White House podium and disparaged Democratic lawmakers while invoking the coming election, dismissing their concerns about artificial intelligence as “nothing but an effort to influence the midterms.”

And on Wednesday, Mr. Blanche spoke at a campaign rally for Michael Whatley, the Republican Senate candidate in North Carolina. Echoing his convention speech, he portrayed crime rates, which continued a long-term downward trend to reach new lows in 2025, as “President Trump and Vice President Vance delivering on a promise.”

Worries about the Justice Department abandoning its long-held commitment to appear apolitical in order to maintain institutional credibility may seem beside the point. Since January 2025, dozens of judges have viewed its representations with suspicion, eroding the traditional bonds of trust, known as the “presumption of regularity,” that the courts typically grant the department.

The second Trump administration has also unabashedly destroyed the post-Watergate norm of Justice Department independence from the White House in investigative decisions. Early on, Mr. Blanche’s predecessor, Pam Bondi, declared, “We are so proud to work at the directive of Donald Trump.” Last September, after Mr. Trump publicly demanded that she charge several perceived adversaries, the department pushed through short-lived indictments of two of them.

Still, Mr. Blanche is dismantling another post-Watergate principle: that Justice Department leaders stay away from partisan politicking.

Joseph Tirrell, the Justice Department’s senior ethics official until the Trump administration dismissed him in July 2025, earlier this week criticized Mr. Blanche’s participation in the Republican convention. He called the attorney general’s comments at the White House briefing “borderline” unethical, and his participation in the North Carolina rally “terrible.”

“In my former role, I would have advised the attorney general not to go to the White House and not to make comments about members of Congress within 45 days of an election,” Mr. Tirrell said. Referring to a law restricting partisan political activity by government employees, he added: “I’d say, ‘That rally sounds like a Hatch Act violation to me, and I’d advise you not to do it.’ I would want to scare that person straight.”

Stephen Gillers, a New York University law professor who specializes in legal ethics, said Mr. Blanche’s political statements and activities were protected by the First Amendment, and did not violate professional conduct rule, even if they were ill-advised.

“Any attempt to discipline him will fail,” Professor Gillers said. “That’s unfortunate. He has the ability to do what he’s doing, and he’s chosen to do it.”

The Justice Department did not respond to a request for comment.

When the group Public Citizen filed a Hatch Act complaint about Mr. Blanche’s comments praising Mr. Blakeman, the Justice Department told Government Executive in a statement that it was “baseless” and “a politically motivated complaint designed to weaponize the Hatch Act against the attorney general for his support of law enforcement.”

And in response to criticism last week by Democrats on the House Judiciary Committee over Mr. Blanche’s convention appearance, the department shot back on social media: “Todd Blanche’s appearance this evening in his personal capacity is legal (and has been approved by ethics).”

Legal questions center on the Hatch Act, which is ambiguous and difficult to enforce when an administration does not want to strictly adhere to it. The law and related regulations allow some political appointees, while off duty, to attend partisan events, like fund-raisers and campaign rallies. Some law enforcement officials are restricted from any partisan activity, but the attorney general is not listed among them, and it is disputed whether that part of the legal limits applies to them.

Even for those who can engage in political activity in a personal capacity, the traditional test is not just whether such officials say they are doing so, but whether people would reasonably perceive them as acting in their government roles.

Cynthia Shaw, who ran the Justice Department’s ethics office throughout Mr. Trump’s first term, said the notion that high-ranking officials could simply say they are acting in a personal capacity to get around that threshold was a misunderstanding.

“The bigger the job you get, the less personal capacity you have, because when you speak, people are going to see you in your official capacity and representing the agency that you are head of,” she said.

Federal law enforcement needs to not just be fair, she added, but to be seen as fair for the long-term good of the department and society.

For that reason, the Justice Department had long held itself to a higher standard than the Hatch Act and its ambiguities. For decades, its ethics policies went beyond the statute in pushing officials to avoid events like political fund-raisers and campaign rallies.

In 2022, Attorney General Merrick B. Garland flatly banned political appointees from participating in partisan activities — even in their personal capacities, and even if their family members were the candidates.

But in March of this year, Ms. Bondi rescinded that policy, freeing political appointees to attend such events in their personal capacities subject only to the lower standards of the Hatch Act.

That weakening of ethics rules is one reason the department’s claim that Mr. Blanche’s appearance at the Republican Party convention was “approved by ethics” merits scrutiny. Another is that the administration has changed who makes ethics recommendations.

After firing Mr. Tirrell, the administration left his position vacant for nearly a year before appointing Kristina Spencer, a former aide to Vice President JD Vance who had no prior department experience.

The office of the deputy attorney general can also overrule the ethics office’s recommendations. For decades, the decision maker was a career official, but the Trump administration moved that authority to political appointees.

The principle that the Justice Department should strive to appear apolitical took root after Watergate. President Richard M. Nixon’s first attorney general, John Mitchell — who later went to prison for his role in the scandal — was so deeply partisan that he resigned to run Nixon’s 1972 re-election campaign.

The attorney general immediately after established the modern norm of not acting as a political operative while in office: Edward Levi, a University of Chicago legal scholar.

Maintaining a nonpartisan image has proved difficult, partly because of the department’s power and an increasingly polarized political atmosphere. Under both parties, one attorney general after another has been accused by political opponents of politicizing the Justice Department.

In 2013, Attorney General Eric H. Holder Jr. called himself President Barack Obama’s “wing man,” clashing with the principle of Justice Department independence. Asked last week about Mr. Blanche’s speech at the Republican convention, Mr. Holder said: “It’s unprecedented, and it’s disgraceful. Attorneys general don’t talk about political things. He shouldn’t be there.”

Mr. Holder, while serving as attorney general, never spoke at the Democratic convention or at campaign rallies. Nor did Republican attorneys general frequently accused by Democrats of politicizing the department, including Attorney General William P. Barr during Mr. Trump’s first term.

Professor Gillers said that shifting standards for the conduct of attorneys general would harm the rule of law, especially if Mr. Blanche’s successors followed his example.

“This is new,” he said. “The changing image of what an attorney general should be seen to do, and how officials high in the Justice Department should behave, will not be good. We just don’t know yet how bad it will be.”

item.title: Virginia Attorney General: D.H.S. May Have Broken State Laws in Voter Fraud Investigation
item.description:
The attorney general of Virginia sent a letter on Thursday warning Markwayne Mullin, the homeland security secretary, that the department’s hunt for evidence of election fraud “potentially violates several Virginia laws” and demanding that the investigation cease immediately.

The New York Times previously reported that hundreds of Homeland Security agents have been assigned to an intensive, weekslong hunt for noncitizens among the nation’s registered voters despite an absence of evidence of widespread fraud. The Times also reported this week that, according to a whistle-blower report, the agents may have broken state laws by effectively posing as voters on public-facing state websites to gain access to individual voting records.

Some states include clear proclamations that the sites and records are meant only for individual use. Virginia is among them. Its voter information portal requires users to check a box attesting: “I certify and affirm that the information provided to access my voter registration is my own or I am expressly authorized by the voter to access this information. I understand that it is unlawful to access the record of any other voter.”

In his letter, Attorney General Jay Jones of Virginia, a Democrat, declared that agents who checked that box while trying to look up voter information may have broken state laws.

“Users that falsely make this certification in an effort to gather protected voter information may be violating several Virginia criminal statutes,” he wrote, citing three Virginia statutes. Because voter registration information and voter history are protected from disclosure by Virginia state law, he added, Homeland Security’s actions required a court order.

Mr. Jones also questioned justifications found in training materials from the office of the chief counsel at the Department of Homeland Security that agents were allowed to use tools to look up state voters for investigatory purposes.

“The Office of the Attorney General of Virginia is not aware of any blanket legal authority that would permit” Homeland Security agents “to obtain protected information from state officials without a court order, let alone any authority that would permit agents to gather that information through fraudulent means.”

As The Times previously reported, agents used personally identifiable information compiled from both internal and external sources, such as birth dates or partial Social Security numbers, to look up voter records on websites that require such information to limit use of the portals to individual voters.

A representative for the Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Rae Pickett, a spokeswoman for Mr. Jones, said in a statement that the office “cannot confirm the existence or scope of investigations,” but confirmed the authenticity of the letter.

“The reported access and use of protected personally identifiable information in a federal search of state voter systems is deeply concerning, particularly because it comes from the highest echelons of government,” Ms. Pickett said in a statement. She added: “The Office of Attorney General is reviewing this troubling report and will take all appropriate actions to preserve Virginians’ private information and the integrity of our elections.”

The Unlawful Voter Initiative, as the Homeland Security investigation is internally known, offers a clear window into the extent to which the federal government, prodded by President Trump’s false claims about American elections, is searching for evidence of fraud ahead of the November elections. The government pulled hundreds of agents from their normal duties, which include investigating serious crimes such as human trafficking and terrorism.

Mr. Jones demanded that the operation be halted and that any records pertaining to Virginia be turned over to his office. He also seized on details from the whistle-blower account released on Monday as evidence that Homeland Security leadership was aware of the legal ramifications.

“The whistle-blower also alleged that” the chief counsel “informed agents that they would not be ‘personally liable for conducting these searches,’ which further suggests that leadership is aware that the underlying conduct violates state law,” Mr. Jones wrote.

item.title: Alabama Executes Inmate After Supreme Court Blocked Last Attempt
item.description:
Alabama used lethal injection on Thursday to carry out the death sentence of a convicted murderer, three months after the U.S. Supreme Court blocked the state from executing the man with nitrogen gas.

Lawyers for the condemned man, Jeffery Lee, had succeeded in raising doubts about the constitutionality of using nitrogen gas in executions, a method that Alabama has been at the forefront of embracing as lethal injection drugs have become harder to obtain. The Supreme Court stopped the execution in a rare intervention on June 11, just as the state was prepared to put Mr. Lee, 49, to death that day using the gas.

The court order did not undermine his death sentence, leaving an opening for the state to try again using another method. State officials quickly rescheduled Mr. Lee’s execution, this time turning to lethal injection. Mr. Lee died just after 6 p.m. Central time at Holman Correctional Facility in Atmore, Ala., state officials said.

“In June, after Mr. Lee attempted to avoid his deserved death sentence, I reaffirmed my commitment that justice would ultimately be served,” Gov. Kay Ivey of Alabama said in a statement on Thursday evening.

Mr. Lee’s death sentence in 2000 came after he tried two years earlier to rob a pawnshop just outside of Selma armed with a sawed-off shotgun. He opened fire inside, killing two people — the owner, a well-known Elvis impersonator named Jimmy Ellis Sr.; and his ex-wife and business partner, Elaine Thompson. A third person, an employee named Helen King, was wounded.

A jury convicted Mr. Lee in the murders and voted to sentence him to life in prison without parole. The trial judge overrode that decision and sentenced him to death, a practice that was outlawed in 2017 but did not apply retroactively.

Alabama was the last state to prohibit the practice. The state still has about two dozen other inmates on death row who, like Mr. Lee, were sent there by judges.

Prominent legal and political figures in the state, including some supporters of the death penalty, had called on Ms. Ivey, a Republican, to spare his life, rather than continue what they cast as an alarming imbalance.

In a statement on Thursday, Mr. Lee’s lawyers condemned the state for moving forward. “That is a moral failure, not just a legal formality,” they said.

“A state that no longer stands behind the rule that condemned a man, but kills him under it anyway, has not delivered justice,” his lawyers said. “It has revealed how little its own standards constrain it when it is determined to carry out an execution.”

But Ms. Ivey defended the executions of Mr. Lee and the other inmates who had been sent to death row under similar circumstances, saying the state was carrying out a punishment that was brought a measure of justice to victims’ families and survivors.

“These victims have waited long enough,” she said, “and I pray they can feel peace and have closure.”

Alabama is among the states that have pressed ahead with executions even as legal and logistical challenges have mounted.

Texas put 40-year-old LeJames Norman to death on Wednesday; he was convicted of fatally shooting three people in 2005 while robbing a home in rural Jackson County, near the Gulf Coast.

Georgia had been set this week to execute Stacey Humphreys, who was convicted of strangling and shooting two real estate agents in a sales office in the Atlanta suburbs in 2003. But his execution was delayed at the last minute as his lawyers sought to have his life spared using a new state law that allows for leniency in sentencing for abuse victims. They argued that Mr. Humphreys, 53, had “suffered extreme violence and abuse as a child.”

For much of his time on death row in Alabama, Mr. Lee had been set to be executed using lethal injection, the state’s primary method for roughly two decades. But that method fell out of favor after botched attempts led the state to pause executions for three months in 2022 and after pharmaceutical companies restricted sales of the drugs.

Alabama introduced the execution method of nitrogen hypoxia, where a person is forced to breathe in only nitrogen gas, asphyxiating them. Mr. Lee was among the condemned inmates who opted for the new method, which had been portrayed by its supporters as efficient and potentially painless. But after the method was introduced in 2024, witnesses described inmates writhing and gasping for air for 10 minutes or longer.

Those accounts led Mr. Lee and other inmates to challenge its constitutionality. In his case, Mr. Lee proposed that he die by firing squad. A federal judge agreed with his argument that marksmen firing directly at his heart would provide a quicker death with a lesser likelihood for pain.

Mr. Lee has acknowledged his guilt, going as far back as the sentencing portion of his trial in 2000. But he has argued that his punishment should be the one the jury wanted.

State officials contend that the execution was a measure of justice for the lives lost and upended after Mr. Lee opened fire in the pawnshop.

In the 26 years that he has been on death row, Mr. Lee has become involved in prison ministry. In an interview this month with The New York Times, as his execution loomed, he reflected on how he had wanted to prove to others, as well as himself, that his life was defined by more than his worst sins.

“Being a good friend, being a good mentor, being a good teacher and preacher of the word of God, being an OK barber,” he said. “I know I am who I’m supposed to be now, and I know what I’m supposed to be doing, and I’m doing it.”

item.title: Jury Reaches Mixed Verdict in Death of Reporter Covering Super Bowl
item.description:
A jury in Louisiana on Thursday found a woman guilty of negligent homicide but acquitted another man of manslaughter in the killing of a sports anchor who was covering the 2025 Super Bowl in New Orleans, prosecutors said.

Danette Colbert, 49, and Rickey White, 35, faced charges of manslaughter and racketeering in the death of Adan Manzano, 27, a journalist for KGKC, the Telemundo affiliate in Kansas City. A third man, Christian Anderson, was also charged in the death, but he accepted a plea deal and testified against his co-defendants in the trial.

Mr. Manzano, who lost his wife in a car accident in 2024 and had a young daughter, had been in New Orleans to cover the matchup between the N.F.L.’s Philadelphia Eagles and the Kansas City Chiefs. It was his third consecutive time covering the Super Bowl for his Spanish-language station.

He was found dead, facedown on a pillow, after his co-workers said he didn’t show up for an appointment. Mr. Manzano died from the combined toxic effects of Xanax, a prescription drug, and alcohol, in addition to positional asphyxia, which is when a person’s body is positioned in a way that prevents breathing.

The jurors, who deliberated for more than five hours, found Ms. Colbert and Mr. White guilty of racketeering, according to the Jefferson Parish District Attorney’s Office. That charge carries a sentence of up to 50 years in prison, the office said, and negligent homicide carries a 10-year term.

The sentencing is set for Sept. 28, according to the office.

Ms. Colbert was the last person seen with Mr. Manzano in his hotel in the New Orleans area. She also stole his credit card and phone, according to the authorities, who added that investigators had found Xanax in her home in Slidell, La.

The three defendants were accused of working together to dupe victims and steal their money. Mr. White acted as Ms. Colbert’s pimp, finding victims for her, the authorities said.

Lawyers for the defendants did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Ms. Colbert worked as a prostitute in the French Quarter, where she found victims and encouraged them to visit an A.T.M., according to prosecutors. She would observe as the person entered their information.

Ms. Colbert would then lure victims back to a hotel room or another “private place” and wait until the person was unconscious after consuming alcohol or drugs or having sex, prosecutors said. She was also charged in similar scams in Las Vegas, but those cases were dismissed.

Ms. Colbert would photograph her victims’ identification information and steal their cash, credit cards, phones, jewelry and other valuables, prosecutors said.

Mr. Anderson, 35, was accused of also acting as a prostitute or aiding Ms. Colbert by providing “technical support” and distributing drugs, prosecutors said. He pleaded guilty to simple robbery and intent to defraud on Thursday, according to the Jefferson Parish District Attorney’s Office, and was sentenced to six years in prison.

Mr. Anderson wrote a letter to the judge, in which he took responsibility for his actions, apologized and asked for mercy.

“In my past, I have surrounded myself with people who were no good for me and let actions, addictions and behaviors influence me in negative ways,” he wrote.

Ms. Colbert was sentenced in May 2025 to 25 years in prison for drugging and robbing another man in 2021.

item.title: S.U.V. Driver Charged With Murder in Los Angeles Bus Crash
item.description:
The driver of an S.U.V. that slammed into a Los Angeles bus on Tuesday evening, killing two people and injuring five others, has been charged with two counts of second-degree murder, prosecutors said Thursday.

The driver, Bailee Lynn Rios, 36, was “impaired by drugs” when she blasted through a red light into opposing traffic and broadsided the bus, the district attorney of Los Angeles County, Nathan J. Hochman, said at a news conference on Thursday.

In addition to murder, Ms. Rios has also been charged with driving under the influence and reckless driving, Mr. Hochman said. She faces a maximum sentence of life in prison.

It was not immediately clear if Ms. Rios had legal representation.

Mr. Hochman said that at around 5 p.m. on Tuesday in Chatsworth, in the San Fernando Valley region of Los Angeles, Ms. Rios was driving a Ford Expedition “well beyond the speed limit” before she plunged into the metro bus.

The collision killed two passengers, Daniel Castillo, 46, and Gage Weida, 31. Another five passengers were injured, two of them critically, Mr. Hochman said, noting that the crash was so severe that two people had been thrown from the bus upon impact.

Stephanie Wiggins, the chief executive of the Los Angeles County Metropolitan Transportation Authority, said at the news conference that the bus driver was among those injured.

Ms. Rios also had “illegal hard drugs” in the car, Mr. Hochman said. He added that the drugs in the vehicle and in her system were still under evaluation.

The crash attracted a swarm of news helicopters, one of which plummeted to the ground and burst into flames, killing its pilot and reporter, as well as a pedestrian on the ground. The helicopter crash has led to soul-searching in Los Angeles County, which has long relied on aerial news gatherers to be the eyes over a vast, sprawling region.

Mr. Hochman said that when the federal investigation into the helicopter crash was complete, prosecutors would “certainly consider” whether or not there was a “tie-in” with the case against Ms. Rios.

“If there is, then we will consider the appropriate charges,” he said. “If there is not, then that will not lead to any further charges.”

Mr. Hochman cited other cases in which people who had driven over the speed limit while under the influence of alcohol or drugs had been charged with murder.

“If you’re thinking about getting behind the wheel drunk or drugged, think again,” Mr. Hochman said.

In another high-profile case in Los Angeles County, Rebecca Grossman, a philanthropist, was convicted of murder in 2024 in the hit-and-run killing of two young brothers in Westlake Village. She struck them in a crosswalk while racing her then boyfriend in her S.U.V., which she was driving while under the influence of drugs and alcohol, according to court records and trial testimony.

Mr. Hochman also referenced a case in which a woman traveling about 130 miles per hour in a Mercedes killed six people in a Los Angeles neighborhood in 2022. That trial is ongoing.

Ms. Rios’s bail has been set at $4.1 million. She will be arraigned on Friday.

item.title: Former Institute of Peace Workers Warn Trump May Push to Engrave Name on Building
item.description:
Former staff members of the U.S. Institute of Peace asked a federal court on Thursday to prevent the Trump administration from carving President Trump’s name into the facade of the headquarters in downtown Washington.

In a filing to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia, lawyers for the institute’s ousted leadership said that engraving Mr. Trump’s name on the building would cause “irreparable harm” because the act would further damage the organization’s independent mission. They argue that mission is separate from the federal government.

Mr. Trump’s name was already adhered on the Institute of Peace in December in large, silver letters alongside the existing engraving of the institute’s name. A White House spokeswoman said at the time that the organization, which has essentially been defunct since March 2025, had been renamed the “Donald J. Trump United States Institute of Peace.”

The White House and the State Department, which manages the building, did not immediately respond to questions about whether there were imminent plans to engrave Mr. Trump’s name there.

Thursday’s motion is the latest development in legal wrangling over the Trump administration’s takeover of the peace-building nonprofit, which included firing staff members and seizing the building with the help of law enforcement authorities.

While legal proceedings continue, the administration maintains control of the institute and its elegant headquarters, which sit along the National Mall. The institute was created by Congress and received federal funding for its programs, though the building was funded through a mix of federal money and private donations.

The lawyers did not say in their filing why they anticipated that the name would be carved into the building. But in the filing they said that they asked the administration to commit to not carving the name while the case is pending, which the government’s lawyers did not do. The government’s lawyers also did not confirm “that no such action would be taken,” the filing said.

Mr. Trump in his second term has sought to name several Washington institutions for himself. Recently, the president blasted a judge’s decision to remove his name from the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts after Mr. Trump handpicked board members who voted to rename it the “Trump-Kennedy Center.”

It is not clear what federal authority would organize an engraving of the Institute of Peace headquarters and pay for it. Though a federal judge ruled last year that the takeover had been a “gross usurpation of power,” a three-judge panel stayed that decision on appeal and returned control of the institute to the administration.

Darren Beattie, who was installed as the head of the institute by the Trump administration, ceded use of the 150,000 square-foot headquarters in November to the State Department, which has used event spaces in the building for Mr. Trump to host world leaders, throw a lavish private dinner party in the president’s honor and serve as an elegant backdrop for speeches.

item.title: Immigration Officer Found Guilty of Sexually Assaulting and Robbing Women
item.description:
A U.S. Customs and Border Protection officer was found guilty on Thursday of sexually assaulting, robbing and threatening four women with a gun at hotels in the Chicago area in 2022.

After a nearly two-week trial, a federal jury in Illinois convicted the officer, Luis Uribe, on all charges, including 10 counts of deprivation of rights and one count of brandishing a firearm.

According to prosecutors, on at least six occasions between February and October 2022 in Schaumburg and Naperville, Ill., Mr. Uribe, who worked at O’Hare International Airport in Chicago at the time, entered the hotel rooms of four women, brandished his badge and threatened them with a firearm issued by Customs and Border Protection.

Mr. Uribe robbed each of the women, who were all of Chinese descent, sexually assaulted two of them and tried to sexually assault the two others, said a spokesman from the U.S. attorney’s office in the Northern District of Illinois. At least two of the women said they were working as prostitutes at the time.

During trial, Mr. Uribe’s lawyers acknowledged that he had visited prostitutes, according to The Chicago Tribune. But they argued that the accusations were false and that the women, who had sought Mr. Uribe’s help with immigration matters, had set him up. Mr. Uribe said from the stand, “I never robbed anybody in my whole life,” and urged that the relations he had with the women were consensual.

Mr. Uribe’s lawyers could not immediately be reached for comment on Thursday.

The verdict came after a federal grand jury indicted Mr. Uribe in December 2025 on the same charges. He was arrested that month and placed in detention, according to the U.S. attorney’s office.

Mr. Uribe’s lawyers tried to get the indictment thrown out, arguing in a motion that the grand jury had been “irreparably tainted” by the misconduct of the prosecutors, including one who “had inappropriate familiarity with grand jurors.” But the judge denied the motion, allowing Mr. Uribe’s trial to proceed.

Mr. Uribe, 45, is a former Marine who has worked for the federal government since 2009, court documents said. He has no history of addiction to alcohol or controlled substances and no mental health issues, the documents said. Mr. Uribe is still employed by Customs and Border Protection, according to the U.S. attorney’s office.

“C.B.P. takes all allegations of employee misconduct seriously,” a Customs and Border Protection spokesman said in a statement on Thursday, adding that the agency is committed to “ensuring that all employees are held to the highest standards of integrity, professionalism and personal conduct.”

Prosecutors said that Mr. Uribe had followed some of the women to their hotel rooms and forced his way in. In one instance, Mr. Uribe threatened a woman, who had moved hotels to avoid him, with a knife and tried to assault her, but was interrupted by a knock at the door, court records show.

According to the court records, in early 2022, a fifth woman, who said she worked as a prostitute, was asked by her boss to meet with Mr. Uribe and take a photo of him to distribute to others as word of his abuse spread. She was also told get Mr. Uribe to agree to stop attacking the women in exchange for free sexual relations. But Mr. Uribe “did not abide by the terms of the bargain,” the documents said.

Mr. Uribe is scheduled to be sentenced on Jan. 21, 2027. He faces a maximum sentence of life in prison and a minimum of seven years.
